utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, as always. And this is the case number, IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Brdjanin, good afternoon to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. General Talic, good afternoon to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Yes, I can hear you in a language that I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Pardon? Could you repeat the last part. I can hear you in a language I can understand. Okay. I just wanted to inform you that Mr. -- you may sit down. You may sit down. I just wanted to inform you that Mr. Zecevic has been appointed as your lead counsel according to a decision taken on the 31st day of May and only communicated to me today. I suppose it has been communicated to you as well, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not yet. But I was informed that a decision was filed today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So General Talic, this is to confirm to you that the lead counsel that you had opted for has been approved and appointed. I also notice that he is currently assigned to represent the accused Simic in the other case that is -- in another case that is pending before this Tribunal and that it is in your interest to have a meeting with Mr. Zecevic -- or Zecevic as early as possible to make sure that he is in a position to give you all the time that you require, because it's not easy to split one's time to two different cases being heard at the same time and for at least half of the year at the same -- at the same -- either morning --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can intervene, there's no problem. I know what's happened in the Simic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I do though. And it's not going to cause any problem as far as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Korner. I thank you for putting my mind at rest at least.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm aware of his position, as I think Madam Fauveau is aware. And it will not cause any difficulty in representing General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. That's very important for me to know. And I'm sure also it puts General Talic's mind at rest, that he will be well looked after. I'm sure that together with Madam Fauveau the team will -- will guarantee your defence as best as possible. Thank you. Yes. I see Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just under the heading of Tribunal amusements, everybody but Madam Fauveau has been notified about Mr. Zecevic and everybody but me has been notified about Mr. Trbojevic as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You haven't received --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No. We never received notice. But everyone else did, so we know that he's been appointed. So I think there must be a policy not to give notice --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And to be frank -- to be frank with you, I was -- I've been asking myself why on earth doesn't Mr. Ackerman introduce Mr. Trbojevic as his co-counsel when he has already been appointed. I think I have the copy here, if you want to have a copy, Mr. Ackerman. I can give you a copy myself, and that would spare me having to go through other channels. Yes. Having -- I will make sure that you have a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, by having raised it, I think it will probably be in my box within the hour, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I suppose so. But it's not something that should happen. I mean -- anyway. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner and -- I keep doing this. Joanna Korner assisted by case manager Denise Gustin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Korner. And good afternoon to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm John Ackerman with my new co-counsel Milan Trbojevic and Marela Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Good afternoon to you. And appearances for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. I'm Natasha Ivanovic-Fauveau, counsel for the accused General Talic, and I'm still alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In actual fact, I am remembering now, Mr. Ackerman, that with regard to your new co-counsel, I myself wasn't handed a copy but Judge Janu was and she gave me hers. So -- so that's how it happens. Anyway, Dr. Sabanovic, good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. May I ask you to stand up and repeat the solemn declaration that you made before this Tribunal yesterday once more.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Madam Korner will continue with her examination-in-chief today. And then the Defence teams will proceed with their cross-examination. In the meantime, Ms. Korner, just to give you and of course the rest an indication of our time schedule for today, we'll be sitting now for the first part until 3.45. Then we'll have a break of 15 minutes, resuming at 4.00. Okay? And after that, we'll stop at 5.15, resuming again at 5.30, and finish at 6.30. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Dr. Sabanovic, I want to start this afternoon with dealing with two of the major transports that came to the camp. First of all, towards the end of July or thereabouts, did trucks arrive carrying people from Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did they arrive in the early evening?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: With an escort of armed policemen, mainly wearing camouflage uniforms but some, I think you said, were wearing former JNA uniforms.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, did the trucks come into the camp that evening?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't enter the camp. They were outside the camp next to the north entrance, the entrance that is to the north of the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And at that stage were Dr. Derviskadic and the nurse, Asim Bajric, called to examine some of the people?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And were you then called out as well?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They called me after everybody had already been examined. There were seven men, and Dr. Derviskadic wasn't quite sure about them because they were in a very poor state. And then medical corps sergeant came, the one who was in charge of Manjaca, and took me outside the camp. I didn't really feel particularly well, but I did go to see those seven patients. Six of them were comatose, that is, they were unconscious. And one could communicate -- and he came from Kamengrad near -- a village near Sanski Most. And since we could communicate, I told them they could stay in our hospital facilities so they could treat them, that we had medicines, and that we could admit them to him. He didn't need any surgical interventions. However, one of the policeman said that they would be taken to the military hospital in Banja Luka. And that patient, that inmate -- or rather, he wasn't that inmate yet. He said that he'd go to Banja Luka. And then I finished the examination of those seven men.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just pause before you go on. Could you see what the cause of their unconsciousness was? Were there any injuries you could see?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Four of them did not have any bodily injuries. They were dehydrated and were in a very bad state because the trip that they had made was done when it was very hot, so that four of them had no injuries and three others had injuries. But these three too were also emaciated, dehydrated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, having finished examining those seven men, were you taken to one of the trucks?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They took me to a truck, to a transporter which had its back door -- its rear door open, and I climbed up. They told me to look at them, and I looked at those bodies. Now --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Pause there. Sorry. Before you tell us about the bodies. When they told you to look at them, first of all who told you, and can you remember the exact words he used?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The exact words of the person who brought me there -- and he is a medical corps sergeant or perhaps he has some higher rank, but he surely is not below corporal. He brought me there because he was sent to fetch me. And he brought me along to protect me and he told me to look at them in that truck, what was in that truck.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did he describe using any particular word what you would find in that truck, or did he tell you who?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, yes. He is an excellent man, and even at the time when he took care of the hygienic conditions in the camp he behaved greatly. And he said that there were people there who had suffocated during the transport between Sanski Most and that place because of the heat, because they had no air, they had simply suffocated for the lack of air on their way to the camp at Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So this was this medical corps corporal or sergeant. Was there anybody else there that you didn't know who said anything to you about the men in the truck?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one was a boy, a young man who was -- studied dentistry and then another one, Biscevic, who was in the camp with me. And before me he had examined those men. Apart from this dentistry student, there was a large number of people who had brought that -- who had escorted that convoy. They were all from the police. And it was a very dramatic, a very grave matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. When you looked inside the truck, you'd been told there were people who had suffocated. What did you see?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw bodies of those people in two rows, and I recognised quite a number of them who were dead. There were 19 -- or 90 of them -- 19, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want you to look, please, at a document that's already been exhibited as Prosecutor's Exhibit 785.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. That was the one that I mentioned that I hadn't put on the list. But we can put the English on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Doctor, I want you to look, please, at the list of people that you can see numbered 1 to 20?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if we could put the English up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have the English version, usher?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Onto the ELMO. The English onto the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner and Ms. Gustin.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Doctor, do you recognise the names of the people who are listed there?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, all of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And are those the people that you saw -- those that you recognised of them on the truck that day?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It appears that some kind of examination was carried out by doctor -- a Dr. Bosko Grubisa and Stanko Erceg. Did you know those doctors?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're my colleagues. Internal medicine doctors. Grubisa used to work with me, somewhat younger. And Dr. Stanko Erceg a specialist in occupational medicine, he worked with me, under me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. If you could take the document away now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, doctor, what happened to the truck with those men on it?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. That truck turned back and drove those men away. They told me there that they were being taken to Sanski Most to be buried there. As I have said, there was this dentistry student. Then there was from the former system a police commander. The police commander who was called Enver Burnic and who frequently came to Manjaca with the police and went back with them. And the two of them likewise that evening together with those dead, they went to Sanski Most as I was told. However, it is not known to this day where they were buried. And the search for the site of their burial still goes on. And these two, the dentistry student --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you pause for a moment I just want to make sure we all understand. There are these dead men on the truck. Then you told us about six men who are unconscious and a seventh who was able to talk to you. In which group was Enver Burnic, the ex-police commander?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Enver Burnic would move about, who communicated with the police, who walked about, like this dentistry student. And those seven and one of them who was conscious and seven unconscious, they said they were taking them to the military hospital in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I'm sorry. Which group did Enver Burnic go with?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He went there with those, with the police who took back the dead in that truck, via Siprica to Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you told us that these men -- do you include in that group Enver Burnic -- had never been seen again? Or I'm sorry. You didn't say that. You said, that it's not known to this day where they are buried.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you ever have a conversation with the camp commandant, Lieutenant Colonel Popovic, about the fate of these men, as to what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And when did you have a conversation?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Popovic told me in confidence that those dead men had been taken to Sanski Most and that they would be buried there. And those who were to go to Banja Luka, that they had never made it to Banja Luka, that they ended in the Vrbas River, that they drowned -- or rather, that they were killed and then thrown into the Vrbas.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So that's those seven men who were drowned in the Vrbas.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can you remember how long after this did Colonel Popovic tell you what had happened to them?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next day. That evening, the next day in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, the other big convoy I want to deal with is the arrival of the Omarska prisoners. Do you remember their arrival?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Roughly how many people were brought from Omarska that you can remember? Although we can find the figure from a document, but ...

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. They arrived in late afternoon at dusk. They were brought by a man from my place who was the police commander in Prijedor, Simo Drljaca. He was head of them. And they also came from the -- by the north gate. And they remained outside that night. And around half past 7.00, I received a list saying that there were 1400 men who had to be examined. That is roughly the figure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. So they were outside the gate. Were they allowed into the camp that night?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you able to examine them that night?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not that night. The next morning, those who were still alive. Not all of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, what happened to those prisoners from Omarska during the course of the night?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was near the stable in which I was; that is, that gate is near this. It was a bastial night of killing, cries of pain, of an experience which one doesn't live through often in -- and yet in wars and unfortunately in a war in Europe it happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you could see what was happening. You've told us you heard cries of pain. What could you actually see was happening, if anything?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could see some -- now and then something, because they would carry out from buses. They had arrived in buses. And they'd take a dead body from the bus now and then. And what happened after that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You tell us you heard cries of pain.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: One or two, or a lot?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It lasted all night. One could not sleep that night. It was sheer horror. That experience was sheer horror.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you examined them the next morning, what did you see? What was the state of the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next day around 11.00 -- and again, the weather was nice. And they were bringing them because many of them could not move. So they brought them out. Those were the severest -- the severest cases of all the inmates who had been brought to Manjaca. They were dehydrated, emaciated, with diarrhoea, high fevers, underweight, and practically unbelievable how they could still live. So the severest, the worst cases who were brought to Manjaca. That was the group in the worst state of all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did any of them have fresh injuries, or did they all appear to be old injuries?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A large number -- when I say a large number, that is 50 to 100 -- had injuries, and more of them. I cannot explain. It was a large group. We never stopped working that day without interruption, because they would be brought in front of the infirmary, those who could move, and they stood. We applied a special system to see what injuries they had suffered. They had not entered the camp yet. Those were not injuries that were inflicted on them in the camp. So there were over 100, I say, with injuries, and they were in a very bad clinical state, all of them, 99 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want you now to look at the -- a video which I think that the unit -- the video unit has got.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's the Ashdown video again, the number of which is P468.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we just pause for one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We can see that none of the men there have their shoes on. Was that an instruction that you were given by the guards?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean an instruction?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In other words --

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. If someone wasn't able to put their shoes on because they had wounds on their feet or was ill, then that would happen. But they weren't wearing their shoes. A lot of people were not wearing their shoes in that barn.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go on then, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And sorry, before we go on. Doctor, if you see anything that you want to make a comment on or anybody that you recognise, could you just ask the operators to pause.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. If we can go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, here the lieutenant colonel called me here. I didn't know that he was there. I was lying about 3 metres away at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, Dr. Sabanovic. One moment. Let's go back a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because I think he wanted -- I notice that he wanted the video to stop even before the Popovic appeared. So let's start it again, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. And if the video operators could stop when they hear the witness begin to speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And let me explain to Dr. Sabanovic exactly what I require. Dr. Sabanovic, look at me. Look at me, please. You are going to have relayed on your monitor a video recording. Now, there may be times, instances, when you will be asked questions. And obviously when that happens, Ms. Korner will ask for the technician to stop -- to freeze the video. But there may be instances where you yourself want to tell us something. To be able to do that, I want you to tell us when to stop, when to freeze the video so that you can make your comments. But you have to say "stop." The moment you say "stop," they will know exactly what they have to do. And then you may proceed with your comments. Okay? So let's start again from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop. You can stop here. I would like to say at this point this gentleman was passing by with the lieutenant colonel, and I was lying behind them to the left from the position I'm looking from. I was on the left, and the lieutenant colonel called to me and he said that I wasn't -- my place wasn't there while the delegation was there and that we would be going to the outpatient clinic. He said I shouldn't be lying in the barn, that we'd be going to the outpatient clinic with our colleagues in order to meet the delegation there. That's what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Pause there for a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop. There is an ill person in this group, someone who was brought to the camp. I think he was one of the most serious cases. All he had was his ribs and his skeleton. I couldn't believe that someone could survive in such a state without some sort of intensive care. Unfortunately -- he was outside later on too. He was lying out -- lying outside. There were flies and other insects. On his body -- he survived, as far as I have heard. Where he is now, I don't know. But that is an example, a living example, of a state where there is only -- where only bones remained and those bones are just covered by skin and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you recognise any of these people?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just pause the video, please. Pause the video. Pause, please.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know these people -- people meet me here, people meet me in Germany in England, when I was part of a delegation in Denmark. Everyone knows me, but I don't know everyone. There are about -- there were several thousand people whom I examined, and I couldn't recognise all those people. And these people are from other municipalities, whom I didn't know. But I got to know them when I examined them later. So I can't say now who everyone is. But in general I know all of them, because I spent six or seven months there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, were you referring to the inmates or the three persons who --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. The people. The inmates. Yes. If we can just finish it off, though I don't think there's anything ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's more or less it. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, doctor, apart from those major transports. During the time you were there, were prisoners brought from a number of different municipalities?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were the major ones, however, Sanski Most and Kljuc and then, of course, the Omarska prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, Sanski Most and Kljuc, and then those people from Omarska, from the camp in Prijedor, three or four camps. And then people were collected in villages. And then from Bosanska Dubica, Bosanska Gradiska, Kotor Varos, and even Banja Luka. But few people from Banja Luka. And then there were people from Croatia. I don't know where they all came from. There were people from all over the place.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I want to ask you about -- a couple of questions about other types of prisoners. But first of all, could you look at three photographs that come from this period, August of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours haven't had this yet. The Defence have got them. If they could be handed to the witness and to Your Honours. And they will become Prosecutor's Exhibit -- okay. There are three, Your Honours, already numbered 808 to 810. Your Honour, they were taken by a photographer who accompanied one of the journalists, as it were, investigations into this. Have we got a spare set anywhere, just so we can put one up on the ELMO, please. Could we put up 808, please, first of all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, doctor, this is a shot taken inside one of the stables. The men that we can see lying there, certainly the two nearest the camera, seem to have some kind of bandaging on their legs.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Their legs are bandaged. Plaster has been put on them. And believe it or not, these people were brought from somewhere - I don't know where they're from - but their bones had been broken. Maybe they jumped out of windows. I don't know what they did. I know them well from sight. And I've spoken to them too. But with your permission, I can say that a man worked on a -- on a church and he fell off and broke his arm. I plastered it. I didn't even take any x-rays. And believe it or not I would meet these people later, and these people weren't even operated on again. These people were brought there and they hadn't been there for long, when they arrived with those plasters -- plaster casts on the right legs of each person.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And so you were able to at least put plaster casts onto people who were injured.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had plaster at the time, and we had bandages, but we didn't have any x-ray machines. So we improvised to the best of our ability.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Could you look, please, then at the next one, 809?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we can put that on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what we're looking at there, Dr. Sabanovic.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, here you can see part of the office there, and you can see the stables on the left. You can see a reservoir which would bring in water. And there are two soldiers behind it, they would bring the water. And you can see this sign where it says "mines." That's what you can see. All this is clear to me. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The water, this tanker or whatever it is. In addition to getting water from the lake, was water brought in then?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This water in the tanker was brought in for -- to use for bathing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How often was it brought in?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very seldom. I didn't have a bath for over two months. I said that on one occasion. But I haven't got anything now. It's resistance. I don't know what.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. And could we look finally, please, at the last photograph, P810. First of all, doctor, that's a shot taken from where? In other words, what are we looking at there? The barns again?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, here you can see a guard who is at the gate. And it says "entrance forbidden." In this -- the person wearing the red article of clothing, that's -- that's me. And this is the person who has to let me go to the command, that is to say, to the clinic, to examine a sergeant or, rather, a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that's me in a good state. That was towards the end. That's me, and that's the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we just establish. You would come through that gate towards where the cameraman was standing, would you, to come to the offices?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And just so we can try and orientate ourselves --

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person in the uniform by the gate, this is someone who guards the gate during the day. And further up there is -- there are the policemen, someone from an observation post. And he opens the gate. And when I am allowed, he will open the gate. We didn't have much freedom of movement then. I would go from the camp to the commander, or rather, to the clinic which is near the command in order to carry out examinations when necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. And just -- just so we can try and orientate ourselves, the main entrance to the camp, was that towards the background or the foreground? In other words, if you wanted to come into the camp, would the gate to the camp be in the again -- through that gate towards where the photographer was standing?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this photograph, this entrance where it says "entrance forbidden, camp" -- it says "camp, entrance forbidden," you can see that on the inside -- if I'm looking at the picture from here, on the inside, there is a man wearing some kind of a suit. You can say some sort of a light military uniform. And I'm wearing this red jacket near the stables and I'm waiting there. So --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But --

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the inside, he will open the gate and I'll go out. That's the main entrance.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that's the only entrance.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the main entrance.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, doctor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You can take those photographs away.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I just want to clear up a couple of matters that I ought to have covered yesterday before we deal with the ICRC and then visitors to the camp. The toilet facilities, what were they?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you putting this question to me?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I am. Yes. I'm sorry. Could you just describe what the toilet facilities were like.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I could. They were next to the exit from the stables. Between the stables there would be two toilet facilities. You would dig a hole which was 10 metres long, 3 metres wide, and 4 metres deep. It would be covered with oak wood, and you'd have about ten openings in the wood and that would be the -- those were the toilet facilities. It's quite simple. You'd then fill it up with earth, when it was full and you'd carry on. These people would just faint, the people from the Red Cross, when they approached the grass where you could smell the urine and everything. That was the worst thing next to those stables, when you had to go to the toilet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was the grass used by the prisoners for anything that was round the toilets?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That grass which grew very well -- it grew very well because it had been fertilised. It grew well, so smokers would take it. They would dry it. And then they would roll it up in -- in a leaf, and they would smoke it. Some of them didn't smoke but some did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you see any prisoner eat the grass?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, no, because if someone did that -- I was there for five days. I didn't eat then. Nothing happened to me. In June it was terrible. But towards the end of July when the Red Cross came, then there were no longer any problems. But perhaps people did that too in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Don't worry.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no limits.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I just wanted to deal with what you actually saw. Did you ever have to provide any sort of medical help to assist people to use the toilets?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we -- we improvised. There were people who weren't able to defecate for three months, over three months. That was terrible. They were in a terrible state. So we would --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think you need to --

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Put him on an elevation. That was terrible. Terrible.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't mean for you to describe in graphic detail what you did. Just simply -- perhaps I can deal with it. Did you provide --

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That has a special name. It's called Kristinrane [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is that effectively, I don't know, an enema? Maybe the translators don't know the word. All right. I think so we've got the general idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think we've got the general idea, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Chamber is satisfied with what the question implies and what the answer more or less implies. Because I think there is a problem with interpretation as you have suggested, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I think there is as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, the arrival of the International Red Cross in July -- I'd like you to look please at a document that's already been looked at, I think, or marked P -- no. It's been marked. P394. Now, this is a document dated the 16th of July, 1992, which is a report on a visit by the International Red Cross to Manjaca, signed in the original, I think, by Lieutenant Colonel Milutin Vukelic. And there's a description of the visit. And if you could look at the second paragraph. There were apparently three people. And said -- it says this: "The entire team broke off today's discussion and visited the camp because apparently they had not been allowed to meet with four prisoners (criminals) on whom a military court had earlier been passed judgement. The representatives were shown their sentences and were even allowed to talk to them freely. They were surprised at this and made observations about the quantities of food, loss of weight of the prisoners, the risk of an epidemic breaking out and the like. They had no valid points to corroborate their observations. And their suggestion to have a group of medical experts examine the prisoners was rejected." I think I'll finish and then ask you the questions. "Specifically they demanded the release of 19 prisoners on account of their state of health. In reality, these individuals were amongst the greatest extremists. They rejected our explanation that these people were guaranteed improved medical care and that they could see for themselves. They brought out accusations at the treatment of the prisoners. They claimed to have seen fresh traces of blood and had no answer to the question of the prison commander as to why they had not allowed a doctor, or one of the prisoners, to establish that immediately." And then it goes -- it says this, after some criticism of the team member's wife. "We demanded that in future they announce their visit at least two to three days in advance, send us a detailed work plan, and do not change the camp's work timetable. Their dissatisfaction is not the result of conditions in the camp but one, our resolve to respect international regulations concerning the treatment of prisoner of war, although they keep on quoting certain articles from that law, thinking that we know nothing about them. They complained of the removal of their equipment, unauthorised release of individuals, a refusal of them to admit they spoke Serbian," and so on and so forth. Now, doctor, first of all, that first visit, were you able to meet the representatives of the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What can I say? I had the opportunity to do so, but I didn't want to and I wasn't allowed to. When I say "I wasn't allowed to," I couldn't intervene personally or ask for anything. I never asked for anything. Because if anyone asked for the Red Cross to provide them with anything, to do something, then you knew what his fate would be. This was quite distorted, this here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry. We'll come back to that. But when you say "they knew what his fate would be," what was happening to people who spoke to the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they would be maltreated, beating in -- during the night. It's impossible to describe that. If they'd asked for someone to be released other for equipment or something like that, no one dared do this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: During the course of that first visit -- there's a reference here to being able to meet -- I'm sorry. Yes. I'm sorry. Yes, there's a reference to being able to meet four prisoners. It's not altogether clear, because first of all the it says, "They'd not allowed to meet with four prisoners criminals on whom a military court had earlier passed judgement." And then it says, "The representatives were shown their sentences, and were allowed to talk to them freely." Do you know who or what that's a reference to, at all?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you what it refers to. There were probably some prisoners who came from the area north of Bosanski Novi, from those parts, but I can't say who they were. I was constantly present there. But I don't know who was sentenced. Nothing was said about that. I don't know. I couldn't provide you with an answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, that document --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Which you can put away.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Again, that can be taken from you. Thank you. Talks about a demand for the release of 19 prisoners on account of their state of health. And I want to move on to the topic of the release of prisoners, if I may. Could we look next, please, at a document numbered P405. I think, doctor, if you get the B/C/S and we have the English up on the ELMO. This is dated the 3rd of August from the 1st Krajina Corps command. And it seems to have been signed on behalf of General Talic. "Approval for the visit of the international committee to the detention camps at Manjaca, Trnopolje, Omarska and Prijedor. On the basis of the verbal order of the Main Staff commander, a visit by the international committee and a team of reporters to detention camps in Manjaca, Trnopolje, Omarska, and Prijedor, within the next two days is approved. In this regard, all measures are to be taken to make conditions in these camps satisfactory. This implies order, cleanliness, functional medical care for the detainees, accurate records of detainees' arrival and release, records of deaths and findings on the cause of death. Wherever representatives of the detainees for contact with the camp authorities have not been selected, this is to be done urgently." And then: "Camp wardens must prepare for briefings." This assignment is urgent and any barring of visits to the camps is out of the question." Now, you've told us you remember, for example, Lord Ashdown coming -- Paddy Ashdown coming round the camp. Do you remember, as it were, a blitz in order to clean up Manjaca before international visitors and reporters arrived?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll tell you briefly. It couldn't be cleaned, nor it was cleaned. You have to do something, either to let off those 19 -- oh, representatives of the camp. Oh, dear. Nobody ever asked anyone. Nobody even tried to do that nor did that happen. And journalists, yes, they did come. And when they come, then -- but I had the occasion to be in the command when they come. But there was no making some order, and there was no cleaning or additional building or something like that. No, there was none of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you remember any selection of prisoners who were supposed to meet any of these international visitors?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, since I went through it, I say it's really funny. Somebody wrote that down. Well, we're not children. That's true. Nobody was ever elected, nor was there any chance of being elected to anything. What bodies? What representatives? Either humane or political or what? There were no elections. You keep your head down and do as you are told. That was it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. That's a slight -- we discussed that yesterday when we looked at the Geneva Conventions document. But when visitors were due to come to the camp, do you recall certain prisoners being selected to talk to the visitors?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never, no one, except the three of us. We enjoyed that privilege, if you can call it that, to talk to CNN, television, Sky News, and all the journalists who came there. For the most part outside the camp in the infirmary, and that's where the television usually came, to the infirmary, and that is where we talked. We would be introduced as inmates, who were the spokesman, if I may make this joke. Others never had a chance. They just there. Journalists come on television go there -- go through that and there were no photographs or anything. Because I was a witness how all these tapes were checked as they were coming out, to decide what could get out, what couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you ever spoke to journalists or to the ICRC, would you complain about the conditions at the camp?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We didn't mention any -- or complain. We were saying that we are calling up on the world to help us survive, because survival is what it was about. And there was -- I mean, people must have been extremely resistant not to die. I told you. Very few people died of natural causes. But we didn't complain to that. We were not allowed to complain. We asked the world to set us free. We were saying that there were five, six, seven, or eight thousand people who were kept beyond any human conditions. And on the CNN, yes I talked with journalists thousands of times. And there was one -- a representative -- the first diplomat who came there, and it was the Minister for Health and Social Welfare of France, Mr. Kouchner, who because of these men who we now saw as a corpse, he said, "Well, take it away. I don't want to look at it." I accompanied him as he visited the camp. So the world also has its skeletons in the closet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So just to be absolutely clear, you never told anyone about the killings or the beatings or all the things you've described to us.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that everywhere I spoke of that, everywhere, except in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Except in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. No. That's what you said?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Except in the camps.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Except in the camps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, doctor. It's my fault. The question wasn't clear enough. All right. Can we also look, please, at the next document very quickly, which shows the build-up, Exhibit P408, please, which to assist will be found immediately after P713 in the Sanski Most binder, Volume 2. It's also in the Banja Luka binder as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we could put the English up, please -- oh, we can't, because it's copied on the back. No. Wrong document. All right. If we just give it to the witness, because it's photocopied on the back.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is dated three days later from the last document, 6th of August. This time it's from the department for intelligence and security of the 1st Krajina Corps, signed by Colonel Stefan Begojevic [phoen]. And it says, "Selection of prisoners in the Manjaca POW camp." And I think we've already looked at this, because Your Honours have already pointed out that one can read the word underneath that's been blacked out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "By processing the war prisoners in Manjaca, we realise that certain, quite large number of them, according to incrimination, do not deserve to be treated as prisoners of war, did not have weapons, did not participate in combat, were not in uniform." Then "in order to free space to accommodate potential new prisoners in Manjaca and in order for each prisoner to get the treatment they deserve, we ask you send a responsible official or several of them to the Manjaca camp, together with the Security Organ carry out a selection of persons who could be released and persons who must remain in the camp. According to our records in Manjaca, there are currently 944 prisoners from Sanski Most. As you know, we have recently been attacked by European and world media in connection with the resistance of concentration camps. So this is sufficient reason to carry out a prisoner selection." Now, first, doctor, were prisoners released after August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, some were released after August -- I mean, after this date. Yes, some were released. But -- may I? There were people released, and they went to England. Then a small group was sent to Banja Luka. Those were over 60 and who were sick. But selection on the basis of these criteria as it said here, no, none of that. But yes, at that time the International Community did begin to bring pressure, and there were about a thousand men from Sanski Most in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you arrange or were you able to arrange for the release of any individual prisoners at all?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, illness once. I was there and I was on that commission when a nurse who used to work there from Banja Luka, and he worked in the camp, I, and at times the investigator -- once I think we let go 15 or 20 men who went to Banja Luka; however, not home. And in the -- earlier, sometime in July, a group of people were taken to Sanica, to the municipality of Kljuc. But what happened to them is another matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You say there was a nurse -- I'm sorry. You said you were on a commission. What are we talking about? What sort of commission? Do you mean a committee?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A commission made of a doctor, a nurse, an official representing the Army of Republika Srpska who ran the camp and one of the investigators. And when I give my opinion about the illness, then the administration -- or rather, the camp command then decided which ones of those would be released, that is, who would be sent to Banja Luka or somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And how often did this happen? I think you mentioned two occasions.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A couple of -- a couple of occasions. A couple of times. Those who left in September to England, I believe - about 20 of them. They were severe cases - they were put on a bus in Manjaca. Then they went to Banja Luka, and from there to England for treatment. And they were let go. And then there was a group that went to Banja Luka and to Donja Sanica, the municipality of Kljuc. I remember those three occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I want you to look at one last document, please, and that's Prosecutor's Exhibit 399.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if we can put the English up on the ELMO very briefly. I'm not going to go through the whole document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is a document from the 1st Krajina Corps, dated the 27th of July and signed by a Colonel Marticic [phoen]. And it's dealing with stepping up security measures and defence of the prisoner of war camp. Order. And it says "on the basis of the demonstrated need to step up security measures in Manjaca prisoner of war camp because of possible interventions and actions aimed at force or liberation of prisoners from the outside or from within, and with a view to organising and taking measures to step up the security and the defence of the camp and prevent actions at liberating the prisoners, I issue the following." And then there's a whole list of things that the camp commander is ordered to do. Was -- did anybody -- well, we know there was no attempt to break in and release people. But did anybody ever attempt to or successfully escape from Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the release, it wasn't like that. Nobody ever tried to release like that. No way. But because of the pressure from abroad, some Chetniks came from outside who at times attacked the camp. So this had to do with it a little bit. But yes, people did flee from Manjaca. A man from Sanski Most escaped. He reached Sanski Most, and in Sanski Most he even paid to go to Bihac, and he reached Bihac and now he lives in Sanski Most. His name is Smajlovic. He does not have one eye. He was a member of the 5th Corps of the BH army in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. You say that because of the pressure from abroad, some Chetniks came from outside who sometimes attacked the camp. What are you talking about there?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But there were already some indications that from around from the neighbourhood -- because there was a big mountain there. So from that area, there's a Chetnik place, has been one since World War II. I mean, everybody -- it's common knowledge that Manjaca were like that. And there were others who were even louder than those who ran the camp, and they were afraid that the camp would be attacked and they would have problems. Not to release people but -- and I know that some people who refused to obey, I suggested that they be sent to the military hospital in Banja Luka. Seven Chetniks who were very unruly, who even refused to obey the rules of those Chetniks who had introduced and imposed a system of warfare. They were even louder. They were even worse.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Can we just try and understand. Are you saying that there were people outside the military, who you call Chetniks, extreme Serbs, who came into the camp?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were such things, but they were always stopped, I must admit, I must say.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Did they get into the camp, or were they stopped by the military before they could get in?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those seven in the early days, whom I mentioned, they were ill-famed. They disagreed even with the existing regime that ruled there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Pause, doctor. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were arrested outside the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And brought to the camp. And I examined them, and they went on a hunger strike. And after the fifth day of the strike, I suggested in order to avoid a certain endocrinological changes in the organism to send them to the Banja Luka hospital. That was done. And although they were notorious Chetniks, they left me alone, they treated me fairly, regardless. But what I said was one fled. Three men came --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Doctor. Just pause. Can we just make this absolutely clear. There were seven extreme Serbs who were outside the camp and they were arrested. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And they were arrested, as you've said, for unruly behaviour. What do you mean? Were they trying to get into the camp? Were they firing weapons? What were they actually doing that led to their arrest?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When they were arrested -- I was told of course I couldn't see that. But I was told that they had been arrested because they did not comply with the rules -- with the regulations of the then authority. They wanted an even more fierce approach to waging the war against those they were waging the war against.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So it was just that they had been arrested by authorities and brought to the camp and imprisoned. Just answer that yes or no, please, doctor.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Were there other Serbs inside Manjaca, apart from these seven men?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. In the camp, there -- yes, there were, a few. From Derventa I know one came. And there was another one -- a short man --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Don't bother to describe them. I just want to know. Were there a number of Serbs in the camp.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, there were a few Serbs. A sergeant one of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what -- did you find out why they were in the camp, what they had done?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because they disagreed with a certain regime.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were any of them there for any other reason other than disagreement with the regime?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've told you. There was a sergeant who had fled from Banja Luka, deserted from the army. He came from somewhere around Nis -- because I had a joke with him. And he headed for Ljubljana, but he was caught and brought to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So he was a deserter. All right. Okay. Finally on the -- before I turn to the visitors on the camp, can I ask you about this. You've described the beatings and the killings. Were there any guards who were particularly brutal that you remember?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you. Distinguished gentlemen, people are different; so are the police. There was one of the worst -- but I do not really condemn the police much. No. I condemn the one who issued orders to the police and who led the police, and that is gospel truth and the reality, because to this day the police do according to the concepts developed by their superiors. And in the camp if they line us up in the so-called line-up from all the stables, then the camp commander, all the investigators and policemen come along, and then you see the police break in like eagles among the little birds and start beating and kicking. There was one called Bula whatever. Those were nicknames. I think they called him Bula or -- a Muslim name. Something. That was his nickname. He was very disagreeable towards others.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The regime you've described of beatings, the deaths, was Popovic the camp Komandant ever present at these beatings?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They allowed it and issued instructions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But when these beatings were -- to your knowledge, was Popovic ever present when one of the men, his men, was carrying out a beating?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a very broad question. When we have these line-ups, lieutenant colonel stands like this and the investigators and the police burst out. Or at night the police come take out somebody and then one can hear screams. This did happen. And that I saw the lieutenant colonel beat somebody, I didn't. But yes, it was with his authorisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah. I'm not asking whether you saw him beat anybody. But I think you've given us the answer. Is there any way he could have failed to be unaware of the deaths that you've described to us?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had to know. He knew everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, do you mind asking the witness whether Colonel Popovic slept the night there, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, you heard -- Doctor, you've heard the Judge's question. Did Colonel Popovic --

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. Your Honour, yes, he did sleep there all the time. He very seldom went to Banja Luka. He'd go there and come back that same day. He slept there in the barracks, or rather, in the camp command. He was present there. He went to Banja Luka very seldom, except for examination when he had a complaint or something. He even offered us, the physician, to sleep where the police slept. But we refused that for safety reasons, because people get drunk and then things can happen. So we preferred to sleep in the stable or in the infirmary, that is, to be with the inmates.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then one final question before the break. Did you ever see -- leave aside General Talic, because I'm going to come to that. But officers of superior rank coming to the camp, superior to Colonel Popovic?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, yes. Before Popovic, there was another lieutenant colonel. I believe he was a Serbian, came from Serbia. He was tall --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Don't --

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And later on, yes, they came. Officers came, majors, and so on and so forth. I don't know much about those ranks., but yes, they did come.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Can we deal with from the time -- I'm sorry. Just to make this absolutely clear. From the time Colonel Popovic was in charge of Manjaca -- if you didn't recognise an officer who was senior in rank, then say so straight away. But did officers senior in rank to him, other than General Talic, visit Manjaca? Or of the same rank I should say.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. No generals came. No generals came, other -- I mean, the way you worded your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What about people of equivalent rank? Would you -- would you be able to recognise someone of equivalent rank; in other words, a lieutenant colonel or a full colonel?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. There were lieutenant colonels, majors, colonels. Yes, they did come.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that would be a convenient moment then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Korner. We will have a break of 15 minutes. If you require more time, please do let me know. If you don't, we can -- we can proceed after 15 minutes -- resume after 15 minutes. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, doctor, I want to deal with some of the Bosnian Serb politicians and the like that visited the camp. First of all, I was asking you about officers who came to the camp, and I excepted General Talic. Now, did you ever see General Talic at the camp?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Not in the camp but in the command of the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And when you say command of the camp, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the part which is outside of the stables where the prisoners were kept.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And how did you know it was General Talic? Had you seen him before that visit?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I'd seen him before. I knew him before the war. I knew him by sight. But I was told that he was there. The policemen told me he was there. I was in the dispensary at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you actually see him arrive?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the officers came to be examined me and he told me that General Talic had arrived in the camp. When he left, I saw him leaving the command. His visit didn't last very long. He didn't spend very much time there when he would visit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And in relation to the command where he went and your infirmary, how close was that?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About -- between 20 and 30 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you said that he didn't spend very much time there when he would visit. Did he visit once or more than once to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he visited on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I know that timing is difficult, but can you remember roughly when those visits were, the month or the time of year?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't pay much attention to the dates or to anything else, but I think it was towards the end of July, maybe August. It was in July or August.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, the next person I want to ask you about is Radoslav Brdjanin. Had you seen him before your imprisonment in Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hadn't seen him, but I saw him on television on one occasion. I didn't see him directly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You mean you didn't see him in real life. You just saw him on television. Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you see him on television once or more than once?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, he said one occasion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he's answered that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once. I saw him once.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. You are right, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you say him, what was -- on television, that is -- what was he doing?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He gave political speeches, political speeches, though -- he talked about mixed marriages, said that that shouldn't be allowed et cetera, and he said similar political things, about the formation of a state. They were political issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You've said he gave political speeches, he talked about mixed marriages. Did he say all of that on the one time that you saw him on television, or did he -- did you hear about other speeches he had made?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear other speeches. That was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So the time you saw him on television, he was making a speech about mixed marriages and similar political things about the formation of a state. That was the one time you saw him.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On that one occasion, the speeches weren't very long. Those were extracts. You know what that looks like. It wasn't a political programme, but it was on the news on television.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, did he ever visit Manjaca whilst you were there?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Once or more than once?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was there once. I am not sure about a second visit. They said that he was there on a second occasion, but I wasn't there. I was in the infirmary. He gave a speech. There was an applause. People applauded, and I then found out that there was an agreement that prisoners -- that is to say, inmates -- should be ordered to listen to the speech. And there was security there. I wasn't able to enter the stables. I was outside because they were already giving the speeches, and people applauded and the applause was greater than at a stadium because there were between 800 and 900 people there. And the speech had to do with the fact that those who were not guilty would be released. But it was emphasised that they would be released to third countries, and those who were guilty would either be sent to a military court and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Let's take this in stages. You're sure of one visit; you're not sure of the second. On the one visit that you're sure of, did you see him at the camp?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And at what stage did you see him? When he came in? When he was in the stable? Where?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he came, I was in the infirmary when he was arriving. But I saw him when he left the second stables, the one in the middle, the central one. Because there are three stables there. That's when I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, how did you know this was Brdjanin? Did you recognise him, or were you told this was Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I was well informed. It wasn't concealed. Nothing was concealed. You know? Brdjanin arrived to visit Manjaca, and that wasn't concealed. He went from one stable to another and he gave speeches. I saw him as he was leaving the second stables.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I know him, like this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. But before that visit, were you told that Radoslav Brdjanin was coming to visit, or on the same day when he arrived?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, before -- before he arrived. There were people there to meet him. It didn't take long. It was all done very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And who was it who informed you before his arrival --

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Police. A policeman or a nurse who worked up there with me -- we were always informed about who was coming, whether it was the TV network, a politician, the police, the army or representatives of the army. That's how things always took place.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you say during that visit he went into the stable, he made speeches, and there was applause.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Who was applauding?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the inmates. They thought they'd be going home that, they'd be released, that they'd go to third countries. When such an offer was made -- well, they were people who were crying then. They thought that they would never get out. But when someone up there in the camp was told that they'd be released from the camp and would be sent anywhere in the world, well, there could have been no greater joy for the people there, no greater joy in the world, because it's a matter of life. If a person is not in a situation in which he thinks he's going to die -- well, I had my head against concrete and I thought I was going to die. So I'm not surprised that people applauded. They were my neighbours, my friends, and they applauded because they were promised that they would be released to third countries.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were there -- I'm sorry. Did Vojo Kupresanin visit the camp?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Had you seen him before his visit, on television or at a rally?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before going to the stables, I'd seen him on several occasion, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Can we --

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before --

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But no, not -- I hadn't seen him before, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. You say he visited the camp, and you said before going to the stables. So did he go to the stables as well?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And how did you know that was Vojo Kupresanin?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in Manjaca I knew who would be visiting the camp. In 99 per cent of the cases, apart from cases which were military secrets, I knew who would be visiting the camp. There would be a visit. I was told that such and such a person would be visiting, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you hear what Vojo Kupresanin -- oh, I'm sorry. Did Vojo Kupresanin speak to the people in the stables?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the same way he -- the speeches were of a similar kind. He said that those who were not guilty would be released, they would go to third countries, that those who were guilty would be sent to military courts. That's a summary. But I only heard a couple of sentences, et cetera, so I couldn't expand on this. That was what the speeches were about in brief.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What about Stojan Zupljanin? Did he visit the camp?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 3 N. It was called 3N, Manjaca 3N. When politicians from the Crisis Staff of the Banja Luka region came.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. What was called 3N?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was called 3N, Kupresanin, Zupljanin, and Brdjanin. All the names finished with the letter N. So that's what they would say, the three N politicians were coming, the three main politicians from the Crisis Staff of Bosanska Krajina or the Serbian republic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And who -- I'm sorry. To be quite clear, who said that to you? The police officer who told you about --

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The inmates would speak about this and even the police. I'd hear it from the inmates, from the police. That's what they would say.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When Zupljanin came -- again, had you ever seen him before or television or in real life?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I hadn't. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what did he do when he was in fact camp?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, he also made speeches. All three politicians would make speeches in the stables. General Talic didn't make a speech.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can you recall any other politicians from the Krajina area, from Banja Luka who visited?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. These were the politicians who came, and it depended on us what -- what would happen. And it depended on -- what would happen depended on them. So I can't really say.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Finally, doctor, I think it's right that you were eventually released from the camp in November of 1992. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. And I was called to the -- summoned to the command where there were several officers, and they told me literally, "You have proved the contrary of what was said about you and you have proved the contrary of what you were charged with." They greeted me and they said that I would be released the following day. Buses arrived, and I was released. I went to Karlovac through Gradiska. A large number left. On that day I was told, as we were leaving, they said, "Take care." Two policemen escorted me on the bus, and one policeman escorted one bus. Two policemen escorted me because they didn't want me to be kidnapped in Banja Luka, because there were telephone calls -- this is what the investigator told me. He told me to be careful, that I would be kidnapped from Sanski Most and that a request had been made for the Serbian people to put me on trial, but I proved that I had never been such a person. I thanked them. I hadn't been traumatised. There were beatings. There were all sorts of things. But I left and I managed to survive. I went to Germany. After the liberation of Sanski Most, I returned. I lived there and worked there. Serbs were returning and others were returning there too. So there's nothing more I could say about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And finally this: Were you joined in Germany by your wife and children? Just answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
